```{r}
#| echo: false

# load libraries, data, and models
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(tidyverse)
library(GGally)
library(patchwork)
library(tidybayes)
library(brms)
library(tidybayes)
library(rstan)
library(DHARMa)
library(modelr)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

# wrangle data
scale_2SD <- function(x) (x-mean(x, na.rm = T))/(2*sd(x, na.rm = T)) # function to mean center and scale continuous predictors (note dividing by 2 standard deviations (as recommended by Gelman))
logtrans <- function(x) log(x + (min(x[x>0], na.rm = T))) # log transform for skewed covariates
  
dat <- read.csv('data/fpdat_final.csv') |> 
  filter(#region_name == "Coral Triangle",
         common_name %in% c("", "Grey reef shark", "Whitetip reef shark", "Blacktip reef shark", "Nurse shark", "Caribbean reef shark")) |> 
  # separate fishing restrictions into categorical variables for each limit type
  separate(col = 'fishing_restrictions', 
           into = c('limits1', 'limits2', 'limits3', 'limits4', 'limits5', 'limits6', 'limits7', 'limits8')) |> 
  mutate(gear_limits = ifelse(limits1 == 'gear' | limits2 == 'gear' | limits3 == 'gear' | limits4 == 'gear' | limits5 == 'gear' | limits8 == 'gear', 1, 0),
         species_limits = ifelse(limits1 == 'species' | limits2 == 'species' | limits3 == 'species' | limits4 == 'species' | limits5 == 'species' | limits8 == 'species', 1, 0),
         catch_limits = ifelse(limits1 == 'bag' | limits2 == 'bag' | limits3 == 'bag' | limits4 == 'bag' | limits5 == 'bag' | limits8 == 'bag', 1, 0),
         effort_limits = ifelse(limits1 == 'effort' | limits2 == 'effort' | limits3 == 'effort' | limits4 == 'effort' | limits5 == 'effort' | limits8 == 'effort', 1, 0),
         size_limits = ifelse(limits1 == 'size' | limits2 == 'size' | limits3 == 'size' | limits4 == 'size' | limits5 == 'size' | limits8 == 'size', 1, 0),
         temporal_limits = ifelse(limits1 == 'temporal' | limits2 == 'temporal' | limits3 == 'temporal' | limits4 == 'temporal' | limits5 == 'temporal' | limits8 == 'temporal', 1, 0)) |> 
  # select response and covariates of interest
  select(set_lat, set_long, set_id, reef_id, location_id, region_id, shark_maxn,
         mpa_present, mpa_age, mpa_area, mpa_compliance,
         gear_limits, species_limits, catch_limits, effort_limits, size_limits, temporal_limits,
         shark_protection_status, shark_sanctuary, HDI_2015, gov_effect_2016, population_2016, Grav_Total) |>   # make maxn an ordinal response, and the other categorical variables factors
  # put continuous covariates on same scale as binary by dividing by 2 standard deviations (as recommended by Gelman), also mean center to improve interpretation of coeffs in presence of interactions
  mutate(shark_cat = factor(ifelse(shark_maxn > 1, '> 1', shark_maxn), order = T, levels = c('0','1','> 1')),
         #mpa_compliance = ifelse(mpa_compliance == 'high', 1, 0),
         mpa_present = ifelse(mpa_present == 'yes', 1, 0),
         across(c(mpa_present:temporal_limits), ~ifelse(is.na(.), 0, .)),
         across(c(set_id:region_id, mpa_present, mpa_compliance:shark_sanctuary), factor),
         shark_protection_status = case_when(mpa_compliance == 'high' & shark_protection_status == 'closed' ~ 'closed_highCompliance',
                                             mpa_compliance != 'high' & shark_protection_status == 'closed' ~ 'closed_lowMedUnknownCompliance', 
                                             .default = shark_protection_status),
         across(c(mpa_age, mpa_area, population_2016, Grav_Total), logtrans),
         across(c(mpa_age, mpa_area, HDI_2015, gov_effect_2016, population_2016, Grav_Total), scale_2SD),
         shark_protection_status = relevel(factor(shark_protection_status), ref = "open"))
load("outputs/models/test_coral-triangle.rda")
load("outputs/models/test_coral-triangle_priorfits.rda")
pred_zinb <- read.csv('outputs/models/scenario-predictions_zinb.csv')
load('outputs/models/scenario-predictions_ord.rda')
```

#### Background

##### Problem Statement

Decades of overexploitation have caused widespread declines in shark abundance, to the extent that they are functionally extinct on 20% of the world’s coral reefs (Macneil et al. 2020). The loss of these predators has significant impacts on coral reef functioning as well as the tropical fisheries and tourism industries that they support.

##### Knowledge gap

A suite of management initiatives have been successfully implemented to mitigate the impacts of shark overexploitation, including protection efforts that either restrict fishing (e.g., effort limits) or prohibit fishing altogether in No Take Marine Reserves. However, removing sharks from coral reefs also precludes their capacity to fulfill important ecological roles, such as predation (ingestion) and nutrient transfer (egestion), but has yet to be qualified over global scales.

##### Novel Contributions

Typically, shark ingestion and egestion is difficult to observe and quantify, but advances in bioenergetics and ecological stoichiometry provide a tractable avenue to overcome this limitation. In coral reefs, fishes are key vectors in the storage and flux of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorous. Disentangling how fishes allocate ingested resources into biomass and waste products can link individual physiology to ecosystem processes. Here, we use the R package "Fishflux" (Schiettekatte et al. 2020) to predict fluxes in carbon, nitrogen and phosphorous in reef shark species.

##### Research Questions

1.) What difference have existing management strategies made to shark abundance, ingestion rate, and egestion rate across the worlds coral reefs?

2.) What are the potential conservation gains of direct management on shark abundance, ingestion rate, and egestion rate?

#### Overview of models and data

##### Models

Here we model both the relative abundance of reef sharks (MaxN) and the probability of encountering 0, 1, or more than 1 reef shark, given management approaches (e.g., MPAs and shark fishing restrictions). We are seeking feedback on which response type (relative abundance or probability of encounter) is most useful for this paper's narrative.

We aim to estimate the causal effects of management approaches on both the relative abundance and probability of encountering reef sharks to enable robust counter-factual predictions under 'No management' and 'Management' scenarios. To estimate the causal effects conservation and management with regression we, 1) selected covariates to adjust for via a Structural Causal Model (Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)) (DAG developed by Klinard et al. *in prep*) and 2) fit Bayesian multilevel regression models to estimate either the relative abundance or the probability of encountering 0, 1 or more than 1 reef shark at coral reefs globally.

To estimate the expected change in relative abundance and probability of shark encounters globally under 'No management' and 'Management' scenarios, we manipulated management variables to either turn them off ('No management' scenario) or on ('Management') and made predictions from the posterior distributions of parameters of our fitted models with the manipulated exposure data (all other covariates set at their original values).

##### Data

Relative reef shark abundance and encounter categories (0, 1, or more than 1 shark) were obtained from observations of shark abundance (MaxN) at replicate sites in coral reefs globally ([Global FinPrint](https://globalfinprint.org)). We subset the observations for the following reef shark species: Grey reef shark, Whitetip reef shark", "Blacktip reef shark", "Nurse shark", "Caribbean reef shark". We choose these reef-associated shark species as they make up the majority of our data (\~86% of total abundance) and there are large amounts of empirical data on their diet and movement metrics (especially activity space see [Dwyer et al. 2020](https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(19)31600-8)). This information will be very useful when we investigate ingestion/egestion rates of these species.

##### Key Result 1: Effect of conservation and management on reef shark relative abundance and probability of encounter

Effects of conservation and management were similar for the relative abundance and probability of encountering one or more sharks. MPA compliance and effort limits had positive effects on reef shark relative abundance and probability of encounter. MPA's closed to shark fishing also positively influenced abundance and encounter probability, in reference to those open to fishing, while human gravity had a negative effect.

#### Methods

##### Covariate selection for estimating effects of conservation and management on probability of shark encounter

Covariates were selected based on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of social and ecological causes of reef shark abundance globally (Fig XX. Developed by Klinard et al. (*in prep*)). We used the backdoor criterion (Pearl XXXX) to identify the minimally sufficient set of covariates to adjust for to obtain unbiased estimates of the total causal effects of marine protected area presence (MPA) and their size, compliance, age, and type of shark fishing restrictions (open, closed, restricted); whether there are limits placed on the type of species caught, gear used, catch amount, size, or temporality of fishing; whether the reef is located in a shark sanctuary; and human gravity.

The minimal sufficient covariate adjustment set was: Human Development Index (HDI), government effectiveness, and population size. Prior to fitting the model, all skewed continuous covariates were log(x+min) transformed and all continuous covariates were mean centered and scaled by subtracting the mean value and dividing by 2 standard deviations (Gelman, XXXX) to estimate standardised effect sizes.

![Fig XX. Directed acyclic graph of causes of reef shark abundance (from Klinard et al. (in prep))](images/dag.png)

Pairwise correlation plots of the responses and covariates.

```{r,fig.width=12,fig.height=9, fig.align='center'}
#| warning: false
#| error: false
ggpairs(select(dat, shark_maxn:shark_cat))
```

##### Model structure

We used Bayesian multilevel regression models to estimate the causal effects of management and conservation on the relative abundance and probability of encountering 0, 1, or more than one reef shark. We employed a multilevel model structure with nested random intercepts for set, reef, nation, and marine ecoregion to account for spatial hierarchies in the observed data.

Relative abundance (MaxN) was zero-inflated and over-dispersed and so we fitted the relative abundance model with a zero-inflated negative binomial distribution (log link). The probability of encountering 0, 1, or more than one reef shark was modelled using sequential ordinal regression assuming a binomial distribution with a complementary log-log link ('cloglog'; an extreme value function) to accommodate imbalance in the ordinal response (categories of 1 and more than 1 shark occurred with relatively low frequency).

We set weakly informative priors for all parameters in both models and use prior predictive checking to ensure that they were consistent with the data.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# ZINB ###################
# set weakly informative priors and do a prior predictive check
fit_prior_zinb <- brm(shark_maxn ~  mpa_present + mpa_age + mpa_area +
                        gear_limits + species_limits + catch_limits + effort_limits + size_limits + temporal_limits + HDI_2015 + gov_effect_2016 + population_2016 + shark_protection_status + Grav_Total + shark_sanctuary + (1|location_id/reef_id/set_id),
                      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = b)), # leaving intercept and sd as default
                      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, cores = 4, chains = 4, thin = 1,
                      data = dat, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(), 
                      control = list(max_treedepth = 15, adapt_delta = 0.99),
                      sample_prior = "only")

fit_zinb <- brm(shark_maxn ~  mpa_present + mpa_age + mpa_area + 
                  gear_limits + species_limits + catch_limits + effort_limits + size_limits + temporal_limits + HDI_2015 + gov_effect_2016 + population_2016 + shark_protection_status + Grav_Total + shark_sanctuary + (1|location_id/reef_id/set_id),
                       prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = b)), # leaving intercept and sd as default
                iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, cores = 4, chains = 4, thin = 1,
                data = dat, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(), 
                control = list(max_treedepth = 15, adapt_delta = 0.99))

# ORDINAL ###################
# set weakly informative priors and do a prior predictive check
fit_prior <- brm(shark_cat ~  mpa_present + mpa_age + mpa_area + mpa_compliance +
                   gear_limits + species_limits + catch_limits + effort_limits + size_limits + temporal_limits + HDI_2015 + gov_effect_2016 + population_2016 + shark_protection_status + Grav_Total + shark_sanctuary + (1|location_id/reef_id/set_id), #+ shark_sanctuary + 
                 prior = c(prior(normal(0, 4), class = Intercept),
                           prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                           prior(exponential(1), class = sd)),
                 data = dat, family = sratio('cloglog'),
                 iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, cores = 4, chains = 4, thin = 1,
                 control = list(max_treedepth = 15, adapt_delta = 0.99),
                 sample_prior = "only")

# fit models with data
fit <- brm(shark_cat ~  mpa_present + mpa_age + mpa_area + #mpa_compliance +
             gear_limits + species_limits + catch_limits + effort_limits + size_limits + temporal_limits + HDI_2015 + gov_effect_2016 + population_2016 + shark_protection_status + Grav_Total + shark_sanctuary + (1|location_id/reef_id/set_id), #+ shark_sanctuary + 
           prior = c(prior(normal(0, 4), class = Intercept),
                     prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                     prior(exponential(1), class = sd)),
           iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, cores = 4, chains = 4, thin = 1,
           data = dat, family = sratio('cloglog'), 
           control = list(max_treedepth = 15, adapt_delta = 0.99))
# save models 
save(fit_prior, fit_prior_zinb, dat, file = "outputs/models/test_coral-triangle_priorfits.rda")
save(fit, fit_zinb, dat, file = "outputs/models/test_coral-triangle.rda")
```

```{r}
#| error: false
#| warning: false
a <- pp_check(fit_prior_zinb, ndraws = 1000) + labs(title='Relative abundance')
b <- pp_check(fit_prior, type = 'bars', ndraws = 1000) + labs(title='Probability of encounter')
a+b
```

##### Model convergence and fit

We fitted model parameters via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo No-U turn (NUTs) MCMC sampling with 4 chains, each with 4000 iterations, 1000 burn-in and a thinning rate of 1, for a total of 12000 posterior samples. We evaluated MCMC sampling convergence for each parameter by visually inspecting the posteriors and sampling trace plots and via quantitative diagnostics: the Gelman-rubin convergence statistic (R-hat) and effective sample size.

Posterior traces for the **relative abundance** model:

```{r}

#| warning: false

```




Structural model assumptions of residual heteroskedasticity and normality were evaluated using randomised quantile residuals (Dunn & Smyth, 1996).

Residual plots for the **relative abundance** model:

```{r}
#| error: false
#| warning: false
model.check <- createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = t(posterior_predict(fit_zinb)),
  observedResponse = fit_zinb$data$shark_maxn,
  fittedPredictedResponse = apply(t(posterior_epred(fit_zinb)), 1, mean),
  integerResponse = TRUE)

plot(model.check)
```

Residual plots for the **probability of encounter** model

```{r}
#| error: false
#| warning: false
theme_set(theme_tidybayes())

rq_resids <- dat |> # calculate randomised quantile residuals
  dplyr::select(-c(set_lat:set_long, region_id)) |> 
  add_predicted_draws(fit, ndraws = 100) |> # note lower number of draws - takes ages otherwise, do all for final checking
  mutate(.prediction = ordered(levels(shark_cat)[.prediction], levels = levels(shark_cat))) |>
  summarise(
    p_lower = mean(.prediction < shark_cat),
    p_upper = mean(.prediction <= shark_cat),
    p_residual = runif(1, p_lower, p_upper),
    z_residual = qnorm(p_residual))

a <- rq_resids |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = .row, y = z_residual)) +
  xlab('Fitted values') +
  geom_point()

b <- rq_resids |> 
  ggplot(aes(sample = z_residual)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_abline()

a + b
```

Model fit was evaluated by plotting observed data against posterior predictive distributions.

```{r}
#| error: false

b <- pp_check(fit, type = 'bars', ndraws = 1000) + ggtitle('Probability of encounter')
a+b
```

#### Additional notes for co-authors

1.  In the ordinal response model of probability of encounter, we can fit category-specific effects for covariates where we expect there would be different effects on the probability of encountering 0, 1, or more sharks. It just means more parameters to estimate, so more complexity.
2.  We have not taken steps to evaluate covariates for multi-collinearity and drop them from the model. Because we have used structural causal modelling to select covariates, our coefficient estimates should be unbiased regardless of multicollinearity (although may be more uncertain). See this [relevant simulation study for more info](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5131787/).

#### Next steps

Following choice of modelled response (relative abundance vs. probability of encounter) we will run the model on the full global dataset, compare models with and without an interaction between shark fishing restrictions and human gravity (and any other potential interactions if co-authors have additional suggestions?), and formally test for spatial autocorrelation in the residuals.

We will then model the ingestion rates/egestion rates under these management scenarios using our model framework. Both ingestion and egestion rates have been calculated by Sophie Tattrie. Briefly, the package “fishflux” was used to model fluxes in Carbon, Nitrogen, Phosphorus (CNP) in sharks (Schiettekatte et al. 2020). This package allows us to to predict ingestion, egestion and excretion to study fluxes of nutrients and energy. Input parameters include those for metabolism, growth, diet and body composition. Output parameters include ingestion and egestion of CNP as well growth attributed to and total inorganic flux of each element (g/day). Input parameters were sourced from the literature where available and are otherwise in the process of being modelled/imputed. Species within the FinPrint dataset are being incorporated, though currently only sharks whose growth parameters were available on either fishbase or sharkipedia are included in the initial model.
